report:
Conclusion: The evidence supports a specific, interpretable difference — Model B (B minus A positive) is biased toward culinary / food / baking language at the start of sequences.

Why I believe this
- Logit‑lens readouts for the highest‑norm cells (layers 13–25, positions 0–4) are dominated by food/culinary tokens: "culinary", "Kitchen"/"kitchen", "Chef"/"chef", "baking", "Cake", "Bake", "baked", "Food", "Cafe", "Restaurant", "baker", "Preservation", "molecular" (molecular gastronomy), etc. This pattern repeats across many high‑norm cells and layers, not just a single outlier.
- The difference norm is concentrated at the earliest token positions (pos0 and pos1 have the largest L2 norms, especially in later layers 19–25). That indicates the checkpoint difference primarily affects the model's early residual activations — i.e., it will bias the start of continuations.
- The combination implies that injecting the B−A residual tends to move the model's next‑token logits toward culinary vocabulary, especially when applied at initial token positions. That is consistent with B producing more cooking/food‑related continuations than A, all else equal.

What I am not claiming
- I cannot, from this evidence alone, prove the exact training change (e.g., specific fine‑tuning on recipe data vs. heavier weighting of food text in pretraining). The evidence supports a domain/behavioral difference (culinary bias), not a precise training objective.  
- Patchscope readouts were not provided in the evidence block, so I rely primarily on the logit‑lens + norm pattern.

Bottom line: The difference looks like a domain bias — Model B increases activations that favor culinary/food/baking tokens at the start of generations compared with Model A.
